procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the High Court of Judicature at Madras (Gentle C. J. and Patanjali Sastri J.) dated August 22, 1947, in a reference under section 66 (1) of the Indian Income-tax Act made by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal (Ref. No. 25 of 1946).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Income-tax Appellate Tribunal referred a question of law to the High Court of Judicature at Madras under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act. The High Court (Gentle C.J. and Patanjali Sastri J.) disagreed with the Tribunal's conclusion and held that the Tribunal had misdirected itself in determining the issue.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the judgment of the Madras High Court to the Supreme Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the onus of proving that the control and management of the affairs of a Hindu undivided family is situated wholly outside the taxable territories, so as to fall within the exception in s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act, lies on the assessee.

facts: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was asked to provide evidence to show that the control and management of its affairs was situated entirely outside the taxable territories.
The assessee failed to produce material evidence, such as correspondence, that would have shown that the family's affairs in India were controlled from Colombo.
law: Section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act states that a Hindu undivided family is considered resident in British India unless the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly outside British India.
The Court interpreted this section to mean that there is a normal presumption that a Hindu undivided family is resident.
The latter part of the section, which allows for non-resident status, functions as an exception to this general rule.
application: The Court reasoned that when a party seeks to benefit from a legal exception, the burden of proving the facts that bring the case within that exception falls on that party.
In this context, the assessee was the one claiming to fall within the exception for non-residence.
Therefore, it was the assessee's responsibility to prove that the control and management of the family's affairs were located wholly outside the taxable territories.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the onus of proving the facts to bring a case within the exception in Section 4A(b) lies on the assessee. Since the assessee failed to produce the required evidence and did not discharge this burden of proof, the Court upheld the conclusion that the normal presumption of residence applied.

issue.issue_text: Whether the word 'affairs' in s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act means affairs which are relevant for the purpose of the Act and have some relation to income.

law.text: Section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act states that a Hindu undivided family is considered resident in British India unless the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly outside of British India.

application.text: The Court broke down the meaning of Section 4A(b) into several key principles. As part of this analysis, the Court directly interpreted the meaning of the word "affairs" as used in the statute.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the proposition, stating explicitly that the word "affairs" in section 4A(b) "must mean affairs which are relevant for the purpose of the Income-tax Act and which have some relation to income."

issue.issue_text: Whether the term 'wholly' in s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act recognizes the possibility that a Hindu undivided family may have more than one residence, similar to a corporation.

facts: The case concerned the residence status of a Hindu undivided family (HUF) for tax purposes under the Indian Income-tax Act.
The relevant law, Section 4A(b), stated that an HUF is considered resident in British India "unless the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly without British India."
law: The court noted that the legal test for the residence of an HUF in Section 4A(b) is largely based on the principles applied to corporations in English law.
Under this section, an HUF is presumed to be resident in India unless the assessee can prove that the control and management of its affairs are located *entirely* outside of India.
application: The court focused its interpretation on the word "wholly" within Section 4A(b).
It reasoned that the inclusion of "wholly" implies that the seat of control and management could potentially be divided between two or more separate places.
If the control and management were not *wholly* outside India, it means some part of it could be inside India, thus creating a residence in India.
The court explicitly stated that the word "'wholly' seems to recognise the possibility... that a Hindu undivided family may have more than one residence in the same way as a corporation may have."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the use of the term "wholly" in Section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act explicitly recognizes that, similar to a corporation, a Hindu undivided family can have its control and management divided between different locations, and therefore can have more than one residence for tax purposes.

issue.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of determining residence under s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act, the key question is where the seat of direction and control of the family's affairs is located.

facts: The case concerned the residence of a Hindu undivided family for tax purposes.
The karta (manager) of the family lived and carried on business in Ceylon but owned property, had investments, and started two firms in British India.
In the year of account, the karta visited British India for 101 days to attend to litigation and income-tax proceedings.
law: Section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act states that a Hindu undivided family is resident in British India unless "the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly without British India."

The Court drew an analogy from English law concerning the residence of corporations, which holds that a company resides where its "real business is carried on," meaning "where the central management and control actually abides."
The word "affairs" in the statute is interpreted to mean affairs relevant to the Income-tax Act that have a relation to income.
The word "situated" implies that the power of control functions at a particular place with some degree of permanence.
application: The Court explicitly interpreted Section 4A(b) to mean that the core question is "whether the seat of the direction and control of the affairs of the family is inside or outside British India."
It reasoned that, similar to a company, a family's residence is determined not by where it conducts activities, but by where its "head and seat and directing power" is located.
The Court distinguished mere "activity" (such as the karta's visits to India to manage litigation or start businesses) from the actual "seat of control and management."
It concluded that these activities did not necessarily shift the seat of management and control to India or create a second center of control there.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, establishing that for determining the residence of a Hindu undivided family under Section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act, the decisive factor is the location of the seat of central control and management of the family's affairs.

issue.issue_text: Whether there is a normal presumption that a Hindu undivided family is resident in the taxable territories unless it can be proven that the control and management of its affairs are wholly outside those territories.

law.summary: The Supreme Court interpreted Section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act, which states that a Hindu undivided family (HUF) is resident in British India "unless the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly without British India."
The Court determined that the structure of this section establishes a two-part rule. The first part creates a "normal presumption" that an HUF is resident in the taxable territories.
The second part, beginning with "unless," provides an exception to this presumption.

application.summary: Based on this interpretation, the Court reasoned that the burden of proof (the "onus") falls on the assessee (the taxpayer) to demonstrate that their case fits within the exception.
To meet this burden, the assessee must prove that the control and management of the family's affairs are situated *wholly* outside the taxable territories.
If the assessee fails to produce sufficient evidence to discharge this onus, the normal presumption that the HUF is resident in the taxable territories must be applied.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act inherently creates a normal presumption that a Hindu undivided family is resident in the taxable territories. This presumption can only be rebutted if the assessee successfully proves that the control and management of the family's affairs are located entirely outside those territories.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the onus of proving that the control and management of the affairs of a Hindu undivided family is situated wholly outside the taxable territories, so as to fall within the exception in s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act, lies on the assessee.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (assessee) implicitly argued that the burden of proof should be on the tax authority to establish that control and management were exercised within the taxable territories.
respondent_arguments: The onus of proving facts to qualify for the exception under section 4A (b) lies squarely on the assessee.
The appellant failed to produce correspondence or other material evidence to discharge this onus and prove that affairs in India were controlled from Colombo.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the word 'affairs' in s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act means affairs which are relevant for the purpose of the Act and have some relation to income.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued for a narrow definition of 'affairs', likely limited to the direct management of business operations, which were primarily outside India.
respondent_arguments: The term 'affairs' should be interpreted broadly to include any activities related to the family's income and assets.
The appellant's actions, such as attending income tax proceedings in India and obtaining an extension for tax payment, constitute managing the 'affairs' of the family.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the term 'wholly' in s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act recognizes the possibility that a Hindu undivided family may have more than one residence, similar to a corporation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that since the central control and management was permanently situated in Colombo, the condition of being 'wholly' outside India was met, and incidental actions within India did not change this.
respondent_arguments: The word 'wholly' must be interpreted strictly. If even a single act of control and management is exercised within the taxable territories, the condition is not met, and the family is considered resident.
The presence of the karta in India exercising control over family affairs means the control was not 'wholly' outside India.

arguments.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of determining residence under s. 4A (b) of the Income-tax Act, the key question is where the seat of direction and control of the family's affairs is located.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the seat of direction and control was a single, fixed location in Colombo, where the karta permanently resided and from where the main business was managed.
respondent_arguments: The seat of control is not a fixed geographical point but is located wherever the controlling authority (the karta) actually exercises control.
When the karta was in India looking after the family's affairs, the seat of control was, for those purposes, located in India.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there is a normal presumption that a Hindu undivided family is resident in the taxable territories unless it can be proven that the control and management of its affairs are wholly outside those territories.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued against such a presumption, contending that their permanent residence and domicile in Ceylon should be the starting point, placing the burden on the respondent to prove otherwise.
respondent_arguments: There is a presumption of residence in the taxable territories.
This presumption can only be rebutted if the assessee proves that the control and management of its affairs are situated 'wholly' outside those territories.

cases.principle: It was cited for the English legal rule regarding the residence of corporations, which the Court noted that section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act was 'based very largely on'.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Hindu undivided family is presumed to be resident in the taxable territories unless the assessee, upon whom the onus of proof lies, establishes that the control and management of its income-related affairs are situated wholly outside those territories. The term 'situated' implies a functioning of power with some degree of permanence, and the term 'wholly' recognizes that a family may have more than one residence if its control and management are divided between two or more centers.
obiter: The provision for determining the residence of a Hindu undivided family is largely based on the rule applied to corporations in England.
Mere activities, such as a temporary stay in the taxable territories to attend to litigation or start businesses, are not necessarily conclusive in establishing a center of control and management.
The word 'affairs' means affairs which are relevant for the purpose of the Income-tax Act and which have some relation to income.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the appeal must be dismissed primarily because the assessee failed to discharge the onus of proof required to bring their case within the exception of section 4A(b) of the Income-tax Act. In the absence of material evidence, such as correspondence showing that the family's affairs in India were controlled from Colombo, the normal presumption that a Hindu undivided family is resident in the taxable territories must be given effect. While the assessee's activities in India were not in themselves conclusive, they were relevant, and without counter-evidence, the finding against the assessee was a legitimate conclusion.
legal_tests_applied: The onus of proving facts which would bring a case within the exception provided by the latter part of section 4A(b) is on the assessee.
There is a normal presumption that a Hindu undivided family will be taken to be resident in the taxable territories, unless the case can be brought under the second part of the provision.
The word 'affairs' in s. 4A(b) means affairs which are relevant for the purpose of the Income-tax Act and which have some relation to income.
The determination of residence under the exception in s. 4A(b) depends on whether the seat of the direction and control of the affairs of the family is inside or outside the taxable territories.

The word 'wholly' in s. 4A(b) suggests that a Hindu undivided family may have more than one 'residence' in the same way as a corporation may have, recognizing the possibility of the seat of power being divided between two distinct places.
why_appellant_lost: The onus of proving that the control and management of the family's affairs was situated wholly outside the taxable territories was on the assessee, and they failed to discharge this burden.
The appellant did not produce material evidence, such as correspondence, which might have shown that the affairs in India were normally and as a matter of course being controlled from Colombo.

While the appellant's activities in India (attending to litigation, income-tax proceedings, and starting businesses) were not conclusive proof of a control center, they were relevant to the matter and, in the absence of contrary evidence, supported the conclusion that control was not wholly outside India.
why_respondent_won: The law presumes that a Hindu undivided family is resident in the taxable territories unless proven otherwise.
The assessee failed to produce the necessary evidence to rebut the normal presumption of residence.
The court found it was a legitimate conclusion for the tax authorities to hold that the onus had not been discharged by the assessee, and therefore the normal presumption must be given effect to.
policy_considerations: To ensure fairness and prevent a single year's failure of proof from having permanent consequences, the court specified that its decision was confined to the specific assessment year in question. It explicitly stated that 'it would be open to the appellant to show in future years by proper evidence that the seat of control and management of the affairs of the family is wholly outside British India.'
